newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - March 21.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Friday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:

* Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group reached a settlement with 22 states over tobacco, acknowledging smoking was addictive. It would also turn over documents which could help anti-tobaccoists in industry litigation.
* Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan hinted at a boost in interest rates next year, as a precaution against inflation.
* The Dow Jones industrials closed down 57.40 at 6820.28 on expectations of higher U.S. interest rates.
* First Bank System said it would buy U.S. Bancorp in a stock swap valued at $8.44 billion.
* A federal jury ordered Dow Jones to pay $223 million libel verdict over a 1993 Wall Street Journal article about now-defunct securities firm MMAR Group.
* Bergen Brunswig terminated its $1.65 billion merger agreement with generic drug maker IVAX.
* Delta's announcement of an exclusive aircraft supply agreement with Boeing provoked a strong response from rival plane-maker Airbus.
* The U.S. trade gap widened by $2.22 billion in January to $12.71 billion, as the deficit with China grew.
* AMR's American Airlines and the pilots union met over a contract settlement but some opposition to the terms was seen within the union.
* New York Stock Exchange short interest rose 5.5 percent in the latest month to 3.1 billion shares.
* Hilton Hotels is eyeing land in Atlantic City where Mirage Resorts and two other casinos are planning a $2 billion project.
* Merrill Lynch realigned its businesses and promoted two executives.
* Mattel said it would take a $275 million charge in the current quarter and lay off 2,700 employees due to its merger with Tyco Toys and restructuring.
* H.F. Ahmanson said it would commit $70 billion in inner-city loans over the next decade if it won a takeover bid for Great Western.
* Heard on the Street: The way the stock market bows down to them, Microsoft and Intel seem to be the market's newest aristocracy.

* Credit markets: Investors bought 30-year bonds and sold shorter-dated Treasury securities yesterday as Wall Street became more convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next week.
